\section[lòushuǐ]{lòushuǐ — to leak water}

\label{lesson:ZH-C522-loushui}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Mandarin for neat and orderly, then the Mandarin for hygiene.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: lòushuǐ}
\emph{lòushuǐ} — \textquotedblleft{}to leak water\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{chúfáng lòushuǐ yǐjīng sān tiān le} — The kitchen has been leaking for three days.
\end{quote}

Its characters come later; for now it is a word for the ear.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{lòushuǐ} is built from \emph{lòu} and \zh{水} 'water', both inherited from Middle Chinese, \emph{luwH} and \emph{sywijX} (Guangyun, in Baxter's transcription). The dictionary glosses the first as the water clock, a vessel that lets water drip away in marked steps; the sense 'to leak' is not given there.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for saying how it was.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{lòushuǐ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{lòushuǐ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chúfáng lòushuǐ yǐjīng sān tiān le} — The kitchen has been leaking for three days.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Mandarin for neat and orderly, then the Mandarin for hygiene, then say \emph{lòushuǐ} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does lòushuǐ mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To leak water\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\zh{上门} (shàngmén)}{上门 (shàngmén)}]{\zh{上门} (shàngmén) — to call at the house (to do a job)}

\label{lesson:ZH-C522-shangmen}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Mandarin for hygiene, then the Mandarin for to leak water.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \zh{上门}}
\textbf{\zh{上门}} — \emph{shàngmén} — \textquotedblleft{}to call at the house (to do a job)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{xiū kōngtiáo de shīfu míngtiān shàngmén} — The man who fixes air conditioners is coming round tomorrow.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\zh{上门}} (\emph{shàngmén}) is built from \zh{上} 'to go up' and \zh{门} 'a door', both inherited from Middle Chinese, \emph{dzyangX} and \emph{mwon} (Guangyun, in Baxter's transcription), which glosses the first 'to climb, to rise': to come up to someone's door.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for saying how it was.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{shàngmén}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{xiū kōngtiáo de shīfu míngtiān shàngmén} — The man who fixes air conditioners is coming round tomorrow.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Mandarin for hygiene, then the Mandarin for to leak water, then say \emph{shàngmén} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[shuǐfèi]{shuǐfèi — water bill}

\label{lesson:ZH-C522-shuifei}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Mandarin for to leak water, then the Mandarin for to call at the house.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: shuǐfèi}
\emph{shuǐfèi} — \textquotedblleft{}water bill\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{zhège yuè de shuǐfèi bǐ shàng ge yuè guì} — This month's water bill is higher than last month's.
\end{quote}

Its characters come later; for now it is a word for the ear.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{shuǐfèi} is built from \zh{水} 'water' and \emph{fèi} 'a cost', both inherited from Middle Chinese, \emph{sywijX} and \emph{phj+jH} (Guangyun, in Baxter's transcription), which glosses the second 'to use up, to spend'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for saying how it was.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[ménlíng]{ménlíng — doorbell}

\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Mandarin for to call at the house, then the Mandarin for the water bill.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ménlíng}
\emph{ménlíng} — \textquotedblleft{}doorbell\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{wǒmen jiā de ménlíng huài le sān tiān le} — Our doorbell has been broken for three days.
\end{quote}

Its characters come later; for now it is a word for the ear.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ménlíng} is built from \zh{门} 'a door' and \emph{líng} 'a bell', both inherited from Middle Chinese, \emph{mwon} and \emph{leng} (Guangyun, in Baxter's transcription), which glosses the second as like a bell, but smaller.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for saying how it was.

\section[dìbǎn]{dìbǎn — the floor of a room; floorboards}

\label{lesson:ZH-C522-diban}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Mandarin for the water bill, then the Mandarin for a doorbell.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dìbǎn}
\emph{dìbǎn} — \textquotedblleft{}the floor of a room; floorboards\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{wǒ shuā le bàntiān dìbǎn} — I spent ages scrubbing the floor.
\end{quote}

Its characters come later; for now it is a word for the ear.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dìbǎn} is built from \zh{地} 'the ground' and \emph{bǎn} 'a board', both inherited from Middle Chinese, \emph{dijH} and \emph{paenX} (Guangyun, in Baxter's transcription), which gives the second as the same word as another spelling glossed, after an older dictionary, 'split wood'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for saying how it was.
\end{grammarlens}
